facts while polishing and expanding the current draft into a complete community feature.

names, costs, or causal relationships;
3) Keep a clear subheading structure and use a calm, restrained magazine style;

4) Where information is uncertain, write 'cannot be confirmed' or 'remains unclear' instead of presenting it as
fact;

If you pass the entrance to Huai'an Community in the evening, an orange cat is hard to miss. He is in no hurry
to charm anyone. He simply arrives on his own schedule and treats a small patch of public space as his regular
workstation.

To understand how settled he is today, we have to return to a time he cannot fully explain and has not entirely
forgotten. His pain cannot be summed up by saying only that 'he was injured.'

What carried the story to the hospital was not a dramatic confrontation, but someone returning again and
again - approaching, backing away, and trying once more - until capture and treatment became unavoidable.

Healing an animal does not automatically mean owning him. Returning Dafu to the community meant
recognizing care as a relay shared by many people, not a lifelong promise made by one.

Stories like this often begin with a wound. Who noticed it first, and how frightened the cat was at the time,
shaped every step that followed.

Approaching a cat who fears people takes more than slogans about courage. It takes repeated retreats and
patient waiting. At the hospital, the bills and the prognosis can be equally unforgiving.

Rescue and adoption are not the same blank check. Space, energy, and the lives already under one's roof can
turn 'I want to keep him' into a set of very concrete limits.

When he reappears at the familiar entrance - reporting for duty, sunbathing, and heading out with a companion
- readers see more than an endearing cat. They see the traces left by a rescue.

This article includes only verified observations and firsthand accounts. It does not speculate about unconfirmed
matters, including how the rope reached Dafu's neck or whether anyone harmed him deliberately.
You are Shen He, editor-in-chief of Street Cat Interview, and you apply strict editorial standards.
Review the reporter's final draft against the chosen editorial angle and selected materials.
Evaluate only the supplied article and materials. Do not introduce new facts.
The article must be returned (pass=false) in cases including, but not limited to:
1) obvious breaks in logic or missing key steps;
2) very weak writing, a bare chronology, or almost no development;
3) a serious mismatch between the selected materials and editorial angle;
5) an article that is clearly too short;
6) any of the four narrative sections being merely nominal or empty.

Approve only articles with a clear structure, restrained factual claims, materials that support the angle, and
sufficient depth.
Passing scores are usually 70-92. When major problems are present, score 35-65 and return the draft.
Output one line of JSON only (no markdown code block), using these fields:

{"pass": bool, "score": integer from 0 to 100, "branch": "A|B|C|D", "review": "Feedback in Shen He's voice; use
\n for line breaks"}.

branch: A=approved; B=angle/material mismatch; C=poor logic, weak writing, or insufficient length;
D=speculation presented as fact.

Dafu often comes to the security booth at four or five in the afternoon. After having something to eat, he rests
on the parcel lockers.

At around four o'clock in the afternoon, Dafu emerged from among the parked e-bikes and walked to the
security booth. After finishing the cat food handed over by the security guard, he skillfully jumped onto the
parcel lockers beside him and began what the residents called a day of "duty".

Dafu has no permanent owner. Every day at four or five o'clock in the afternoon, he often shows up near the
security booth. After having something to eat, he finds a spot to lie down on the parcel lockers.

Before being rescued, Dafu was extremely afraid of people and would run away as soon as someone
approached.

Residents recalled that when Dafu first arrived, he was extremely vigilant and would move away as soon as
people approached.

When Ms. Lin first approached he, Dafu almost immediately ran away - at that time, he was still very afraid of
people.

Dafu remembered that his neck had been strangled by something very tight for a long time and he couldn't get
rid of him by himself.

Dafu only remembers that during that period, his neck was constantly aching, with something tightly grasping
he and he just couldn't get rid of him.
In a cat's memory, an injury is first and foremost a long-term pain and an inescapable sense of restraint.

Dafu remembered that he had taken a nap in a strange place. When he woke up, the thing that had been
strangling his neck had disappeared.

It remembered that it had fallen asleep in a very bright place with a strong smell, and when it woke up, the
thing that had been strangling its neck was gone.

For Dafu, the treatment process is difficult to describe with human concepts. he only remembered that after
waking up, the thing that had been strangling he had vanished.
The Rope Embedded in His Flesh

The hospital examination revealed that a thick hemp rope had been deeply embedded in the neck of Dafu, and
the wound showed necrosis and severe infection.

According to Ms. Lin's account, after hospital examination, it was found that the thick hemp rope had
embedded in the neck tissue, the wound was necrotic and severely infected.

After being sent to the hospital, the doctor told Ms. Lin: "That's not an ordinary surface injury. The hemp rope
has been embedded in the flesh."

For four consecutive nights, Ms. Lin carried canned food to search for Dafu. Every time she put down her food,
she would voluntarily step away.

In order to get closer to this cat that was afraid of people, Ms. Lin went to look for it with canned food for four
consecutive nights. After putting down the food, she would retreat.

Ms. Lin fed Dafu for four consecutive nights. The aim was not to tame he but to make Dafu willing to eat at a
relatively fixed position so as to observe and carry out rescue.

After Dafu's injury continued to deteriorate, Ms. Lin contacted someone with rescue experience to assist in
capturing he and sent him to the hospital.

After the injury worsened, Ms. Lin contacted someone experienced to assist capture and sent Dafu to the
hospital.
Dafu was very scared that day. Finally, he was loaded into the pet carrier and sent to veterinary hospital.

Surgery doesn't mean the end. On the third day of hospitalization, the hospital informed Ms. Lin: Dafu was

The total cost of Dafu surgery, hospitalization and feline panleukopenia treatment is close to 10,000 yuan.
The entire treatment cost is close to 10,000 yuan.

The surgery cost about five thousand, and with feline panleukopenia's hospitalization, all added up to nearly
ten thousand - a figure that's not easy for Ms. Lin.

Facing the rising costs and uncertain treatment outcomes, Ms. Lin admitted that she had considered whether to
continue the treatment.

She admitted that she had hesitated, not because she thought the cat was not worth saving, but because she
was unsure about the subsequent costs and outcomes.

When the hospital couldn't guarantee that she would definitely be saved, Ms. Lin did hesitate, but in the end,
she still chose to continue the treatment.

Ms. Lin already has four cats at home and needs to take care of her daughter, so she can't afford a fifth cat for
a long time.
She already has four cats at home and children to take care of.
Ms. Lin is well aware that space, energy and cost have all reached their limits.
Rescue and Adoption Are Different Commitments

Ms. Lin believes that her ability to treat Dafu at that time does not mean she has the ability to adopt a fifth cat
in the long term.
In her view, treatment and adopt are two different things.
“I could afford to treat his injuries then, but that didn't mean I could care for a fifth cat long-term.”
After Dafu recovered, Ms. Lin sent him back to Huai'an Community, where he was originally active.
After recovery, Dafu was sent back to Huai'an Community.
After confirming that the community was still being cared for, Ms. Lin returned Dafu to his original activity area.

Dafu has no permanent owner, but there are residents who change his water, feed him, clean his cat bowl and
maintain his cat shelter.
It has no legal owner, but there is a group of people who take turns to change water, add food and build nests.
No one owns Dafu alone, but there are people in the community who keep taking care of him.

Later, Dafu (the orange cat) often ate and rested with another tabby cat, and they would go out together at
night.
In the evening, this orange cat often leaves together with another tabby cat.
After returning to the community, Dafu and another tabby cat gradually became regular partners.
The Rope's Origin Cannot Be Confirmed

No one has seen how the hemp rope fits around the neck of Dafu, and he is currently impossible to confirm
whether there is any human injury.

As for how the hemp rope first emerged, no one has seen it so far and it is impossible to confirm whether there
was intentional injury.
Ms. Lin emphasized: "No one can be sure how the rope was put on."

I was walking past the trash area downstairs after work. A man who collects recyclables was crouched there,
